title: CBA REVAMP’S HIDDEN STING
full_text:
The nation’s biggest bank made a song and dance last week about revamping the loyalty program underpinning its credit cards.
Commonwealth Bank flew journalists to Sydney and rolled out executives from Virgin, Woolworths and Myer to talk up the benefits of its “reimagined” points scheme.
Lost in the hype about CBA’s mission to help customers save was one crucial detail. Millions of credit card customers are about to be hit with higher fees.
The pitch was heavy on how customers will be rewarded for everyday banking. Hold a CBA mortgage, savings account or insurance policy, and you’ll earn points.
Use your credit card, and you can unlock value through Woolworths’ Everyday Rewards, Myer or Virgin’s Velocity program.
It sounds like a bonanza.
But if you’re a credit card customer who has been meeting minimum spend requirements to dodge fees, the game is up.
Cashbacks that once cut loan fees, or put money straight back on to credit cards, are gone too.
For disciplined users who paid off their balance and hit spending thresholds to waive fees, the old scheme was genuinely attractive.
In its place is a complicated points system whereby value depends heavily on your customer tier. Diamond customers earn 1.5 points per dollar spent. Regular Yello customers earn just 0.5 points.
Points enthusiasts might enjoy dissecting the fine print to maximise value. For everyone else, it’s a time-sucking maze.
I use an Ultimate Awards card. From January, no matter how much I spend each month, that card will cost me $35 a month. That’s $420 a year.
If I want to convert points to Virgin Velocity? Add another $99 annually. Qantas points? That’ll be $149.
Currently, I use the Awards points to redeem at Myer.
My back-of-envelope calculations show, under the new regime, I’d need to spend $70,000 a year on the card just to recoup the $420 in fees.
There may be better value in using points with other retailers, but I’ve simply chosen to do the maths on what it takes to break even using the Myer option under the revamp.
CBA says more fine print will be released before the new scheme’s launch date on October 1. Maybe more value still lurks in those yet-to-be-released details.
For now, CBA points to opportunities in earning on electricity bills, mobile plans and car insurance.
But let’s be clear about what’s happening here. This “reimagining” is marketing spin designed to dress up a fee hike, conveniently timed ahead of the Reserve Bank’s October 1 ban on credit card surcharges.
CBA wouldn’t dare frame it that way, though. Instead, the bank is trumpeting the new value customers are about to receive. For Ultimate credit card holders, there’s a monthly $25 credit for something called Travel Booking.
Then there’s $10 monthly towards Dine In Deals, a partnership with food app EatClub, and an annual DoorDash membership worth $120, in case you’d like to spend even more on getting dinner delivered.
If you’ll genuinely use these perks, good luck to you.
But to my thinking, when you strip away the packaging, this is a fee waiver replaced by incentives to spend more.
Some customers might consider that a fair trade. For disciplined credit card users, it’s a downgrade dressed up as an upgrade.
CBA is no orphan in this scramble. NAB and Westpac have already reworked their points schemes. ANZ has slashed sign-on bonuses.
The banks are working hard to ensure they don’t take a profit hit from the regulatory change.
The Reserve Bank estimates the surcharge ban will strip roughly $660m from bank revenue nationally.
But the banks clearly have other ideas.
If you’re a huge fan of frequent flyer schemes, maybe this offers another way to rack up points you need for those elusive seats available on dates you weren’t all that fond of travelling on via a route that will take twice as long. Power to you.
For me, who uses a credit card as a budgeting tool and is never slugged interest and fees, it’s a different story.
I’m now reimagining my money strategy. Is there a better card out there? Should I shift to debit, or even cash? If you haven’t checked what’s changing on your card, now is the time. The banks are counting on us not to examine the fine print.
